title: New species have appeared slowly and successively on land and in the sea

fields.label: Label
fields.value: New species have appeared slowly and successively on land and in the sea

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: New species have appeared very slowly and one after another, both on land and in the waters, rather than in simultaneous batches.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: New species have appeared very slowly, one after another, both on the land and in the waters.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On the slow and successive appearance of new species”. Scope: terrestrial and aquatic species in the fossil record, especially Tertiary

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-01: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.81

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The variables and alternatives map directly to standard paleobiological analyses. Global coverage is imperfect, but sufficient data exist to evaluate whether clustered pulses or slow succession better describe major intervals.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Estimate taxon first-appearance rates and clustering through time separately for terrestrial and aquatic records after standardizing sampling. Compare gradual asynchronous origination against simultaneous pulses at available temporal resolution.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Preservation differs sharply between land and water.

Stage-level dating can make gradual appearances look simultaneous.

fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.86
operationalizability: 0.85
data adequacy: 0.76
discriminating power: 0.62
data existence: 0.94

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Origination series are a standard Paleobiology Database analysis and can be run quickly with sampling standardization. They resolve genus-level marine turnover, especially in the Cenozoic, and leave species-level and terrestrial succession weakly covered. Bin length and sampling spikes keep the test from isolating truly simultaneous batches.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: In terrestrial and marine occurrence data, test whether first appearances are spread across successive time bins or clustered in the same short horizons. A staggered sequence supports successive appearance; repeated pulses of many unrelated first appearances, beyond sampling spikes, would challenge it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The terrestrial record is much patchier than the marine record, and bedding-scale collecting spikes imitate simultaneous origin.

Geological stages are coarser than one-after-another within a formation.

The record is mostly genera, so species-level succession is a proxy.
